SEO_Body:
Net Profit Margin Calculator

Use our Net Profit Margin Calculator to quickly calculate your net profit margin as a percentage. Simply enter your total revenue and total costs to see how much of your revenue remains as profit after costs.

Understanding Net Profit Margin

Net profit margin displays the percentage of revenue remaining after subtracting all operating expenses, taxes, interest, and costs of goods sold. A higher margin can indicate better expense control and financial sustainability.

Net Profit Margin Formula

Net Profit Margin = ((Total Revenue - Total Costs) / Total Revenue) * 100

For example, if a business generates £100,000 in revenue and has total costs of £80,000, its net profit is £20,000 and its net profit margin is 20%.

How to Calculate Net Profit Margin

To calculate your net profit margin, enter your total revenue and total costs into the calculator. The calculator subtracts your costs from your revenue to determine your net profit, then expresses that profit as a percentage of your total revenue.

What Does Net Profit Margin Tell You?

Net profit margin helps show how much profit a business retains from each pound of revenue after accounting for its costs. For example, a 15% net profit margin means that a business keeps £15 in net profit for every £100 of revenue.

Comparing net profit margins over time can help businesses understand changes in profitability and assess the impact of increasing revenue, reducing costs or changing operating expenses.

Net Margin vs Gross Profit Margin

Gross profit margin measures the profit remaining after the cost of goods sold, while net profit margin takes a broader view and accounts for additional expenses such as operating costs, interest and taxes. Net profit margin therefore provides a more complete picture of overall profitability.

Calculate Your Net Margin

Enter your revenue and costs into the Net Profit Margin Calculator above to calculate your net profit and net margin percentage. It's a simple way to assess profitability and understand how much of your revenue remains after costs.

Weight and Mass Conversion

Accurate weight conversion is crucial for shipping, cooking, fitness tracking, and scientific calculations. Easily convert between standard metric units like kilograms and grams or imperial units like pounds, ounces, and stones.

Common Weight Conversion Rates

  • 1 Kilogram = 2.20462 Pounds
  • 1 Pound = 16 Ounces
  • 1 Stone = 14 Pounds (6.35029 Kilograms)

How to convert kilograms to stones and pounds

Body weight in the UK is often given in stones and pounds. To convert from kilograms, multiply by 2.20462 to get pounds, then divide by 14. The whole number is the stones and the remainder is the pounds. For example, 70 kg is 154.3 lb, which is almost exactly 11 stone.

About the units

  • Kilograms: The base unit of mass in the metric system. Used for body weight, groceries and luggage in most of the world.
  • Grams: One thousandth of a kilogram. Used for food ingredients, post and small items.
  • Milligrams: One thousandth of a gram. Used for medicine doses and nutrition labels.
  • Tonnes: 1,000 kilograms. Used for vehicles, freight and building materials.
  • Pounds: The main imperial unit of weight, written lb. There are 14 pounds in a stone.
  • Ounces: One sixteenth of a pound, written oz. Used in recipes and for small parcels.
  • Stones: 14 pounds. Used in the UK and Ireland for body weight.

Frequently asked questions

Is weight the same as mass?

In everyday use, yes. Strictly, mass is the amount of matter in an object and weight is the force of gravity on it, but scales are set up to show mass.

Is a tonne the same as a ton?

Not quite. A metric tonne is 1,000 kg. The UK long ton is 1,016 kg and the US short ton is 907 kg.

Speed and Velocity Conversion

Converting speed measurements is vital for travel planning, aviation, maritime navigation, and sports analytics. Effortlessly switch between terrestrial speeds (mph, km/h) and nautical or aviation units (knots).

Common Speed Conversion Rates

  • 1 Mile per Hour (mph) = 1.60934 Kilometers per Hour (km/h)
  • 1 Knot = 1.15078 Miles per Hour (mph)
  • 1 Meter per Second (m/s) = 3.6 Kilometers per Hour (km/h)

How to convert mph to km/h

Multiply miles per hour by 1.609 to get kilometres per hour, or divide km/h by 1.609 to get mph. A rough rule that is easy to do in your head: multiply mph by 8 and divide by 5. The UK motorway limit of 70 mph is 112.7 km/h, and a 30 mph limit is 48.3 km/h.

Where each unit is used

If you drive abroad, speed limits will almost always be in km/h, and a British car's speedometer usually shows both scales. Runners and cyclists tend to think in pace or km/h, weather forecasts give wind in mph or knots, and physics problems use metres per second.

  • Kilometres per hour: Used for road speeds in most countries, written km/h.
  • Miles per hour: Used for road speeds in the UK and the United States.
  • Metres per second: The scientific unit of speed. Also used for wind speed.
  • Knots: One nautical mile per hour. Used at sea and in aviation.
  • Feet per second: Used in engineering and ballistics, mainly in the United States.

Frequently asked questions

Why is a knot different from a mile per hour?

A knot is based on the nautical mile, which is 1,852 metres. An ordinary mile is 1,609 metres, so a knot is about 15% faster than 1 mph.

How fast is 100 km/h in mph?

About 62 mph.

Temperature Conversion

Temperature conversions are widely used in cooking, weather forecasting, science, and engineering. Easily convert between Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin.

Common Temperature Formulas

  • Fahrenheit to Celsius: (°F - 32) × 5/9 = °C
  • Celsius to Fahrenheit: (°C × 9/5) + 32 = °F
  • Celsius to Kelvin: °C + 273.15 = K

A quick way to estimate

To turn Celsius into Fahrenheit in your head, double it and add 30. The result is close enough for weather: 20 °C becomes 70 °F by this method, against a true figure of 68 °F. To go the other way, subtract 30 and halve.

Worked example

A recipe from the United States says to bake at 350 °F. Subtract 32 to get 318, multiply by 5 to get 1,590, and divide by 9 to get 176.7 °C. On a British oven you would set 180 °C, or 160 °C for a fan oven.

  • Celsius (°C): Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Used for weather and everyday temperatures in the UK and most of the world.
  • Fahrenheit (°F): Water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F. Used in the United States and still seen on older British ovens and thermometers.
  • Kelvin (K): The scientific scale, which starts at absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible. A change of one kelvin is the same size as a change of one degree Celsius.

Frequently asked questions

At what temperature are Celsius and Fahrenheit the same?

At minus 40. It is the one point where the two scales cross.

Why is there no degree sign for kelvin?

The kelvin is a unit in its own right, so temperatures are written as 300 K, not 300 °K.

Is centigrade the same as Celsius?

Yes. Centigrade is the older name for the Celsius scale.

Cooking and Baking Measurement Conversion

Accurate kitchen measurements ensure recipe success whether baking or cooking. Easily convert between volumetric units like cups and tablespoons, liquid volume like milliliters, and dry weight measurements like grams and ounces.

  • 1 Cup = 16 Tablespoons = 240 Milliliters
  • 1 Tablespoon = 3 Teaspoons = 15 Milliliters
  • 1 Fluid Ounce = 29.57 Milliliters

Cups measure volume, not weight

This converter changes one volume into another. It cannot tell you what a cup of an ingredient weighs, because that depends on the ingredient: a cup of water weighs about 240 g, a cup of plain flour about 120 g and a cup of granulated sugar about 200 g. For baking, weighing ingredients in grams is more reliable than measuring by the cup.

Following an American recipe

American recipes use the US cup of 240 ml, along with US fluid ounces and US pints, which are smaller than the British ones. A US pint is 473 ml and a UK pint is 568 ml. Spoon sizes are effectively the same on both sides of the Atlantic.

SEO_Body:
How to convert watts to amps

The current an appliance draws, in amps, is its power in watts divided by the voltage of the supply. Watts measure how fast energy is used, volts measure the electrical pressure and amps measure the flow of electricity.

Watts to amps formula

Amps = Watts / Volts

Worked example

A 2,000 watt fan heater is plugged into a UK socket at 230 volts. Dividing 2,000 by 230 gives 8.7 amps, comfortably within the 13 amp limit of a standard plug.

Common appliances at 230 volts

60 W0.26 ATelevision or laptop charger
800 W3.5 AMicrowave oven
1,200 W5.2 AVacuum cleaner or hairdryer
2,000 W8.7 AFan heater
3,000 W13.0 AKettle
7,200 W31.3 AElectric vehicle home charger

Why the current matters

  • Fuses. A UK plug takes a fuse of up to 13 amps. Appliances under about 700 watts normally use a 3 amp fuse, and larger ones a 13 amp fuse.
  • Extension leads. Add up the current of everything plugged into a lead. The total must not exceed its rating, usually 13 amps.
  • Circuits. Large loads such as cookers, showers and car chargers need their own circuit with a suitably rated cable and breaker.

Motors and electronics

The formula is exact for heaters, kettles and other simple resistive loads. Appliances with motors or electronic power supplies draw a little more current than their wattage suggests, because of power factor. The current on the rating plate is the figure to rely on.

Frequently asked questions

What voltage should I enter?

230 volts for UK and European mains, 120 volts for North America, or 12 volts for most car and caravan systems.

Can I use this to choose a cable size?

No. Cable sizing also depends on the length of the run, how the cable is installed and the protective device. That is a job for a qualified electrician.

Meta_Desc: Estimate the yearly running cost of a fridge or freezer from its energy label class and your electricity price. Compare classes A to G.
Intro_Text: Choose the energy class of a fridge or freezer and enter your electricity price to estimate what it costs to run each year.
SEO_Body:
What a fridge costs to run

A fridge or freezer is switched on every hour of the year, so its efficiency has more effect on your bill than almost any other appliance. The energy label gives the electricity it uses in a year, in kilowatt-hours. Multiply that by the price you pay per kilowatt-hour and you have the yearly running cost.

Running cost formula

Yearly cost = Annual energy use (kWh) x Price per kWh

Worked example

A fridge freezer uses 240 kWh a year. At 28p per kWh, it costs 240 x £0.28, which is £67.20 a year. A model that uses 150 kWh a year would cost £42, a saving of £25.20 every year for as long as you own it.

Energy classes A to G

Fridges and freezers sold in the UK carry a label with a class from A, the most efficient, to G, the least. The scale was reset in 2021, replacing the old A+, A++ and A+++ ratings, and the new classes are much stricter. An appliance that was A+++ under the old scheme may be a C or D today, so the two cannot be compared directly.

The calculator uses a typical yearly consumption for each class. The class boundaries depend on the size and type of appliance, so a large American-style fridge freezer uses more electricity than a small under-counter fridge of the same class. For an accurate figure, use the kWh per year printed on the label of the model you are looking at.

Is a more efficient fridge worth the extra?

Compare the difference in price with the difference in running cost over the life of the appliance. A fridge freezer commonly lasts ten years or more. A model that costs £80 more to buy but saves £25 a year pays back the difference in just over three years and saves money after that.

Ways to cut the running cost

  • Set the fridge to between 3 °C and 5 °C and the freezer to minus 18 °C. Colder than that wastes electricity.
  • Leave a gap behind the appliance so air can move over the coils.
  • Check that door seals close tightly, and let hot food cool before you put it in.
  • Defrost a freezer that is not frost-free when ice builds up.
Short_Desc: Estimate a fridge's yearly running cost from its energy label.

What is gross profit margin?

Gross profit margin is the share of your selling price that is left once you have paid for the goods themselves. It ignores overheads such as rent, wages and marketing, so it tells you how profitable the product is before the costs of running the business are taken off.

The calculator works for a single item or for a whole period: enter one product's cost and price, or your total cost of goods sold and total sales.

Gross profit margin formula

Gross profit = Selling price - Cost of goods

Gross profit margin = Gross profit / Selling price x 100

Worked example

You buy a lamp for £60 and sell it for £100 before VAT. Your gross profit is £40, so your gross margin is 40%. The same sale has a markup of 66.67%, because markup is measured against the cost and margin against the selling price.

What is a good gross margin?

It depends on the trade. Grocers and electronics retailers often work on low margins and high volumes, while clothing, furniture and software businesses usually need much higher margins to cover their overheads. The most useful comparison is with your own figures from earlier periods, and with the margin you need to cover your fixed costs.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter what the product costs you, including delivery to you and any duty.
  2. Enter the price you sell it for, without VAT.
  3. Read off the margin, the profit in pounds and the equivalent markup.

To check a whole month or year, enter your total cost of goods sold and your total sales instead of a single item.

Frequently asked questions

Should I include VAT?

No. If you are VAT registered, use prices and costs without VAT, because the VAT you charge is not your income.

Can gross margin be more than 100%?

No. Margin is a share of the selling price, so it can never pass 100%. Markup can, and often does.

Why is my margin negative?

The cost is higher than the selling price, so each sale loses money before overheads.

What is markup?

Markup is the amount you add to the cost of a product to reach its selling price, shown as a percentage of the cost. It is the usual way for wholesalers, tradespeople and shops to set prices, because you normally know the cost first.

Markup formula

Selling price = Cost x (1 + Markup / 100)

Markup = (Selling price - Cost) / Cost x 100

Worked example

A product costs you £40 and you add a markup of 50%. The selling price is £60, which gives a profit of £20 on each sale. That profit is 33.33% of the selling price, so the margin is lower than the markup.

Markup and margin are not the same

Both describe the same profit, measured against different numbers. Markup compares profit with cost. Margin compares profit with the selling price. A 50% markup is a 33.33% margin, and a 100% markup is a 50% margin. Mixing the two up is a common reason for prices that look profitable but are not.

How to choose a markup

Start with the costs the markup has to cover. Add up your overheads for a year and divide by the number of items you expect to sell: that is the amount each sale must contribute before you make any profit. Then check what competitors charge. If the price your markup produces is well above the market, look at the cost first, because a lower markup may not cover your overheads.

Frequently asked questions

What markup do I need for a 50% margin?

100%. You have to double the cost for half of the selling price to be profit.

Does markup include overheads?

Only if you build them into the cost. A markup on the purchase price alone has to be high enough to pay for rent, wages, delivery and payment fees as well.

Pricing from a target margin

If your business needs a set margin to cover its overheads, the price has to be worked back from the cost. Adding the margin percentage on top of the cost is a common mistake: adding 40% to a cost gives a margin of only 28.57%.

Selling price formula

Selling price = Cost / (1 - Margin / 100)

Worked example

An item costs you £30 and you want a margin of 40%. The selling price needs to be £50. Each sale then earns £20, which is a markup of 66.67% on the cost.

Before you set the price

  • Count every cost. Include delivery to you, packaging, payment fees and marketplace commission, not only the purchase price.
  • Add VAT afterwards. If you are VAT registered, the result is the price before VAT.
  • Check the market. The calculator shows what you need to charge. Customers and competitors decide whether you can.

A VAT invoice must show the net amount, the rate, the VAT and the total for each line or for the invoice as a whole. If you are VAT registered, the VAT you charge is collected on behalf of HMRC and paid over in your VAT return, less the VAT you have paid on your own purchases.

Frequently asked questions

How do I take VAT off a price?

Don't subtract 20%. Divide the price by 1.2 instead, or use our Reverse VAT Calculator.

Do I have to charge VAT?

Only if your business is registered for VAT. Registration is compulsory once your taxable turnover passes the threshold set by HMRC.
Short_Desc: Add 20%, 5% or 0% VAT to a net price.

SEO_Body:
How to remove VAT from a price

VAT is added to the net price, so it has to be taken off by dividing, not by subtracting a percentage of the total.

Net price = Price including VAT / (1 + Rate / 100)

At the standard rate that means dividing by 1.2. At the reduced rate, divide by 1.05.

Worked example

A receipt shows £120 including VAT at 20%. The price before VAT is £100 and the VAT is £20.

The mistake to avoid

Taking 20% off a VAT-inclusive price gives the wrong answer. 20% of £120 is £24, but the VAT in £120 is only £20, because the 20% was charged on the net price of £100. A quick check: at the standard rate, the VAT is always one sixth of the total.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the total price, including VAT.
  2. Choose the VAT rate that was charged.
  3. The calculator shows the price before VAT and the amount of VAT in the total.

The VAT fraction

Accountants often use a shortcut called the VAT fraction to find the VAT in a total. At 20% the fraction is 1/6, so the VAT is the total divided by 6. At 5% the fraction is 1/21. The calculator gives the same answer by dividing the total by 1 plus the rate.

Why is the VAT not 20% of the total?

Because 20% was added to the net price, which is smaller than the total. As a share of the total, VAT at the standard rate is 16.67%.

When you need to reverse VAT

  • Working out your margin from a retail price that includes VAT.
  • Recording the net cost of a purchase when the receipt only shows the total.
  • Comparing a supplier's ex-VAT quote with a price that includes VAT.

Discount formula

Saving = Original price x Discount / 100

Sale price = Original price - Saving

Worked example

An item priced at £80 with 25% off is reduced by £20, so the sale price is £60.

What a discount does to your margin

A discount comes straight out of your profit, because your costs stay the same. If an item costs you £60 and sells for £80, your profit is £20. Take 25% off and the price drops to £60: the whole profit has gone, even though the discount was only a quarter of the price.

Before running a promotion, work out how many extra sales you need for the lower profit per sale to add up to more profit overall.

How to use the calculator

For a quick estimate without the calculator, find 10% by moving the decimal point one place to the left, then multiply. 30% off £80 is three lots of £8, so £24 off.

Percentage off and money off

A percentage discount is worth more on expensive items and less on cheap ones, while a fixed amount off is the same on every order. Retailers often find that a money-off offer sounds better on higher prices (£50 off a £400 item) and a percentage sounds better on lower prices (25% off a £20 item), even where the saving is similar.

Frequently asked questions

How do stacked discounts work?

They are applied one after another, not added together. 20% off followed by a further 10% off is 28% off in total, not 30%.

How do I find the original price from a sale price?

Divide the sale price by (1 - discount / 100). An item that costs £60 after 25% off was £80.

What is the break-even point?

The break-even point is the number of sales at which your income exactly covers your costs. Below it you make a loss. Every sale above it adds to profit.

Break-even formula

Break-even units = Fixed costs / (Selling price - Variable cost per unit)

The amount in brackets is the contribution: what each sale puts towards your fixed costs.

Worked example

Your fixed costs are £5,000 a month. You sell at £25 and each unit costs you £15, so each sale contributes £10. You need to sell 500 units a month to break even, which is £12,500 of sales.

Fixed and variable costs

  • Fixed costs stay the same however much you sell: rent, salaries, insurance, software subscriptions.
  • Variable costs rise with each sale: stock, packaging, postage, card fees and marketplace commission.

How to use the calculator

  1. Add up the costs you pay whether or not you sell anything, for a month or a year, and enter them as fixed costs.
  2. Enter the price of one unit, without VAT.
  3. Enter the costs that each sale causes.
  4. Read off the number of units and the sales value needed to cover everything.

Break-even with a profit target

To find the sales needed for a target profit, add the profit to your fixed costs before you divide. With fixed costs of £5,000, a target profit of £2,000 and a contribution of £10 per unit, you need to sell 700 units: 500 to break even and 200 more for the profit.

If you sell several products, use the average price and average variable cost weighted by how many of each you sell, or work out break-even for each product line with its own share of the fixed costs.

How to lower your break-even point

There are three ways: raise the price, cut the variable cost of each unit, or reduce fixed costs. Change the figures above to see which makes the most difference to your business.

Why is no result shown?

If the variable cost is the same as or higher than the price, each sale loses money and no number of sales will cover the fixed costs.
Short_Desc: How many sales you need to cover your costs.

SEO_Body:
What is contribution margin?

Contribution margin is what is left from a sale after paying the costs that sale caused. That money goes towards fixed costs first, and becomes profit once they are covered.

Contribution margin formula

Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit

Contribution margin ratio = Contribution per unit / Selling price x 100

Worked example

You sell a product for £50 and each one costs £30 in stock, packaging and delivery. Each sale contributes £20, a ratio of 40%. Selling 400 units gives a total contribution of £8,000. If your fixed costs are below that figure, the rest is profit.

How to use it

  • Compare products. The product with the highest contribution per unit is not always the best seller, but it does the most for profit per sale.
  • Judge a discount. A price cut reduces contribution by the full amount of the cut.
  • Find break-even. Divide fixed costs by the contribution per unit.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the selling price of one unit, without VAT.
  2. Enter the variable cost of one unit: stock, packaging, postage, payment fees and commission.
  3. Enter how many units you sell in the period.

The result shows what one sale contributes, the same figure as a percentage of the price, and the total contribution from all the units.

Using contribution to make decisions

Contribution is most useful where a decision changes sales volume but not fixed costs. Should you accept a one-off order at a lower price? If the price is above the variable cost, the order adds contribution and makes you better off, provided it does not take capacity from full-price sales. Should you drop a product that appears to lose money after overheads are shared out? If its contribution is positive, dropping it will make profit worse, because the overheads remain and one source of contribution is gone.

Contribution margin and gross margin

Gross margin takes off the cost of goods sold, which can include some fixed production costs. Contribution margin takes off only costs that change with each sale, and includes selling costs such as commission and postage.
Short_Desc: Contribution per unit, contribution ratio and total contribution.

Percentage change formula

Percentage change = (New price - Old price) / Old price x 100

A positive result is an increase and a negative result is a decrease.

Worked example

A supplier raises a price from £40 to £46. The difference is £6, which is an increase of 15%.

Passing on a cost increase

If a supplier's price goes up and you raise your own price by the same number of pounds, your profit per sale stays the same but your margin falls slightly. If you raise your price by the same percentage, your margin stays the same and your profit per sale rises. Decide which you are aiming for before you reprice.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the price before the change.
  2. Enter the price after the change.
  3. Read off the difference in pounds and the percentage change.

If the new price is lower, both results are shown as negative numbers.

Price rises and inflation

Comparing a price rise with the rate of inflation shows whether it is a real increase. If inflation is 3% and a supplier raises prices by 3%, the price has stayed the same in real terms. A rise of 8% in the same year is a real increase of about 5%. The same check applies to your own prices: a price held flat for several years has fallen in real terms, while your costs have probably risen.

Frequently asked questions

Why isn't a 15% rise cancelled out by a 15% cut?

The two percentages are taken from different starting prices. £40 plus 15% is £46, but £46 less 15% is £39.10.

Can I use this for costs or wages?

Yes. The sum is the same for any two amounts.

SEO_Body:
What is sell-through rate?

Sell-through rate is the percentage of the stock you bought that you have sold in a given period. Retailers use it to judge how well a product, range or season is selling, usually over a month.

Sell-through rate formula

Sell-through rate = Units sold / Units received x 100

Worked example

You took delivery of 500 units at the start of the month and sold 320. Your sell-through rate is 64%, with 180 units still in stock.

Reading the result

A high rate means stock is turning into cash quickly, and may mean you could have sold more. A low rate means money is tied up in stock that might need discounting to clear. What counts as good depends on the product: fashion lines are expected to sell through within a season, while spare parts may sell slowly for years.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the number of units you received or had in stock at the start of the period.
  2. Enter the number sold in the same period.
  3. Read off the sell-through rate and the units left.

Count units, not pounds, and use the same period for both figures.

Acting on the result

  • Above target: reorder before you run out, and consider whether the price is too low.
  • On target: the buy was about right. Use the same quantity as a starting point next time.
  • Below target: improve the listing or display first, then promote the line, and mark it down if it still does not move. Stock that sits costs money in storage and ties up cash you could spend on lines that sell.

Tracking sell-through by product and by week shows which lines to back early in a season, when there is still time to act.

Frequently asked questions

What period should I measure?

Use the same period every time, so results can be compared. A month is the most common.

How is it different from stock turnover?

Sell-through looks at one delivery or period and counts units. Stock turnover compares the cost of everything sold with the average value of stock held, usually across a year.
Short_Desc: The share of received stock that has been sold.

What is stock turnover?

Stock turnover, also called inventory turnover, is the number of times in a year that a business sells and replaces its stock. It shows how hard the money tied up in stock is working.

Stock turnover formula

Stock turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average stock value

Days in stock = 365 / Stock turnover

Average stock is usually the opening stock plus the closing stock, divided by two. Both figures should be at cost, not at selling price.

Worked example

Your cost of goods sold for the year is £240,000 and you hold £40,000 of stock on average. Your stock turns over 6x a year, so an item sits on the shelf for about 61 days before it sells.

Is a higher turnover better?

Usually, because less cash is tied up and less stock goes out of date. A very high figure can also mean you are holding too little and running out. Supermarkets turn stock many times a year. Furniture and jewellery shops turn it far more slowly.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter your cost of goods sold for the year, from your accounts.
  2. Enter the average value of stock held, at cost. Add the opening and closing stock and divide by two, or average your monthly stock counts for a better figure.
  3. Read off how many times stock turns over and the average number of days an item is held.

Stock turnover and cash

Stock is cash sitting on a shelf. A business with £40,000 of stock turning 6 times a year could run on about £30,000 of stock if it turned 8 times, which frees £10,000 for other uses. Faster turnover also cuts the cost of storage, insurance, damage and stock going out of date.

Why use cost of goods sold and not sales?

Stock is valued at cost, so comparing it with sales, which include your margin, would overstate the turnover.

How to improve it

  • Order smaller quantities more often.
  • Clear slow lines with promotions.
  • Use sales history to buy closer to real demand.

SEO_Body:
What is GMROI?

GMROI stands for gross margin return on inventory investment. It tells a retailer how many pounds of gross profit were earned for each pound held in stock, so it combines margin and stock turnover in one figure.

GMROI formula

GMROI = Gross profit / Average stock cost

Worked example

A shop makes £90,000 of gross profit in a year while holding £30,000 of stock on average. Its GMROI is 3.00: every £1 of stock earned £3.00 of gross profit.

How to read it

A GMROI above 1 means the stock earned more gross profit than it cost to hold. Below 1, it earned less. A product with a modest margin that sells quickly can have a better GMROI than a high-margin product that sits on the shelf, which is why the figure is useful for deciding what to stock and how much space to give it.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the gross profit for the period: sales less cost of goods sold.
  2. Enter the average stock held over the same period, at cost.
  3. Read off the GMROI as a number and as a percentage.

You can run it for the whole business, a department or a single product, as long as both figures cover the same thing.

Two ways to improve GMROI

GMROI is the result of margin and stock turnover working together, so there are two levers. Raising margin, by buying better or pricing higher, increases the profit from the same stock. Raising turnover, by holding less or selling faster, earns the same profit from less stock. A line with a 30% margin that turns 8 times a year earns more per pound invested than a line with a 50% margin that turns twice.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a good GMROI?

It varies by sector, so compare products, categories or shops within your own business first.

Should stock be at cost or retail value?

At cost. Using retail value would understate the return.

What is safety stock?

Safety stock is the extra stock you keep in case sales are higher than expected or a delivery arrives late. It is a buffer against running out.

Safety stock formula

This calculator uses the average and maximum method:

Safety stock = (Maximum daily sales x Maximum lead time) - (Average daily sales x Average lead time)

Reorder point = (Average daily sales x Average lead time) + Safety stock

Worked example

You normally sell 20 units a day and your supplier normally takes 7 days to deliver. On your busiest days you sell 30 units, and the slowest delivery took 10 days. You should hold 160 units of safety stock and place a new order when stock falls to 300 units.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter how many units you sell on a normal day and on your busiest days.
  2. Enter your supplier's normal delivery time and the longest it has taken.
  3. Read off the safety stock to hold and the stock level at which to reorder.

Take the figures from your sales and delivery records for the last few months, not from memory.

Safety stock and the reorder point

The two results do different jobs. Safety stock is the buffer you hope not to use. The reorder point is the trigger: when stock falls to that level, there is enough left to cover normal sales while the delivery is on its way, with the safety stock in reserve.

Is there a more precise method?

Yes. Larger businesses use a statistical method based on how much demand and lead time vary, and on the service level they want. The average and maximum method used here is simpler and works well for small ranges.

Things to bear in mind

  • The method covers the worst case you have already seen. It cannot predict a bigger spike or a longer delay.
  • More safety stock means more cash tied up and more storage, so review the figures when sales patterns change.
  • Seasonal products need different figures at different times of year.

SEO_Body:
What is cost of goods sold?

Cost of goods sold, or COGS, is the direct cost of the products you sold in a period. Taking it away from your sales gives your gross profit. In UK accounts it is usually called cost of sales.

COGS formula

Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock

Worked example

You start the year with £12,000 of stock, buy £45,000 more, and have £15,000 left at the end. Your cost of goods sold is £42,000.

What counts towards COGS?

  • Included: the purchase price of stock, delivery to you, import duty, raw materials and direct production labour.
  • Not included: rent, marketing, office salaries and the cost of delivering to customers. These are overheads.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the value of stock at the start of the period, at cost.
  2. Enter the cost of stock bought or made during the period.
  3. Enter the value of stock left at the end, from a stock count.
  4. Read off the cost of the goods you sold.

From COGS to gross profit

Subtract cost of goods sold from your sales for the same period and you have gross profit. In the example above, sales of £70,000 less COGS of £42,000 leaves a gross profit of £28,000, a gross margin of 40%.

How should stock be valued?

At what it cost you, or at what you could sell it for if that is lower. Damaged or obsolete stock should be written down. UK businesses commonly use the first in, first out method, which assumes the oldest stock is sold first.

Frequently asked questions

Why does closing stock reduce COGS?

Stock you still hold has not been sold, so its cost belongs to a later period.

Does a service business have COGS?

Often not, or it is called cost of sales and covers the direct cost of delivering the service, such as subcontractors.

Sales commission formula

Commission = Sales value x Commission rate / 100

Total pay = Base pay + Commission

Worked example

A salesperson sells £25,000 in a month on a commission rate of 5%. They earn £1,250 in commission. With base pay of £2,000, their total pay for the month is £3,250 before tax.

Common commission structures

  • Flat rate: the same percentage on every sale, as this calculator uses.
  • Tiered: the rate rises once sales pass a target.
  • Margin based: commission is paid on the profit from a sale, not its value, which discourages heavy discounting.
  • Commission only: no base pay.

Designing a commission plan

A good plan is simple enough for a salesperson to work out their own pay. Decide what you want to reward: revenue, profit, new customers or renewals. Paying on revenue alone can encourage discounting, so many businesses pay on gross profit or reduce the rate on discounted deals. Decide also when commission is earned: when the order is placed, when it is invoiced or when the customer pays.

Commission and the minimum wage

In the UK, a worker's total pay, including commission, must still come to at least the National Minimum Wage for the hours worked in each pay period. An employer has to top up the pay of a commission-only worker whose sales fall short in a slow month.

Is commission taxed?

Yes. In the UK it is treated as earnings and taxed through payroll in the same way as salary.

Should commission be paid on the price with or without VAT?

Normally without VAT, because VAT is not the company's income. Your contract or commission plan should say.

What is average order value?

Average order value, or AOV, is the average amount a customer spends each time they order. Online shops track it alongside traffic and conversion rate, because together those three numbers decide revenue.

Average order value = Revenue / Number of orders

Worked example

Your shop takes £18,000 from 450 orders in a month. Your average order value is £40.

Ways to raise AOV

  • Set a free delivery threshold a little above your current AOV.
  • Offer bundles or multi-buy prices.
  • Suggest related products on the product page and in the basket.
  • Show a better version of the product next to the one being viewed.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter your revenue for a period, such as a month.
  2. Enter the number of orders in the same period.

AOV and revenue

Online revenue is the product of three numbers: visitors, conversion rate and average order value. With 10,000 visitors, a 2% conversion rate and an AOV of £40, revenue is £8,000. Raising AOV to £44 adds £800 without a single extra visitor or order.

Bear in mind that an average can hide a lot. A few very large orders can pull it up while most customers spend much less, so look at the spread of order values as well. Compare AOV by channel, device and customer type to see where the valuable orders come from.

Mean and median order value

AOV is a mean, so one very large order can pull it up. The median, the middle order when all are ranked by value, shows what a typical customer spends. If the two differ widely, a few big orders are skewing the average.

Frequently asked questions

Is AOV the same as revenue per customer?

No. One customer may order several times. AOV is measured per order.

Should I include delivery charges and VAT?

Either is fine, as long as you measure it the same way every time.

ROAS means return on ad spend: the revenue earned for every pound spent on advertising. It is the standard way to compare campaigns on Google Ads, Meta, Amazon and other platforms.

Worked example

A campaign costs £1,500 and brings in £6,000 of sales. The ROAS is 4x, or 400%: each £1 of advertising produced £4 of revenue.

What ROAS do you need?

ROAS measures revenue, not profit, so the figure you need depends on your margin. Your break-even ROAS is 1 divided by your gross margin. With a 25% margin you need a ROAS of 4x just to cover the cost of the goods and the adverts. With a 50% margin, 2x is enough.

What is CPA?

CPA, cost per acquisition (or cost per action), is the average amount you pay in advertising for each conversion. A conversion is whatever you count as success: a sale, a sign-up, an enquiry or an app install.

CPA formula

CPA = Campaign cost / Number of conversions

Worked example

You spend £1,200 on a campaign that produces 48 orders. Your CPA is £25.

Is your CPA affordable?

Compare it with the profit from a conversion. If an average order leaves £40 of gross profit, a CPA of £25 still makes money on the first sale, while a CPA of £50 only pays back if customers return and buy again. Working out customer lifetime value shows how much you can afford to pay.

  2. Enter the number of conversions it produced in that period.
  3. Read off the cost of each conversion.

Decide what counts as a conversion before you start, and keep to it, so campaigns can be compared.

Target CPA

A target CPA is the most you are willing to pay for a conversion. To set one, start with the profit from a conversion and decide how much of it you are prepared to spend on advertising. If an order leaves £40 of gross profit and you want to keep half, your target CPA is £20. Most ad platforms let you enter a target CPA and will adjust bids to try to meet it.

CPA for leads

If a conversion is an enquiry, not a sale, divide the CPA by the share of leads that become customers. A lead CPA of £10 with one lead in five converting is a customer cost of £50.

How to lower CPA

  • Pause keywords, audiences and placements that spend without converting.
  • Improve the landing page so more visitors convert.
  • Test new adverts regularly against your best performer.

What is CPM?

CPM is the cost of one thousand impressions of an advert. The M is the Roman numeral for a thousand. It is how display, video, social and print advertising is usually priced, and it lets you compare the cost of reaching an audience across different channels.

CPM formula

CPM = Ad cost / Impressions x 1,000

Worked example

An advert costs £450 and is shown 150,000 times. The CPM is £3.

CPM, CPC and CPA

CPM measures the cost of being seen, CPC the cost of a click and CPA the cost of a conversion. CPM suits campaigns that aim to build awareness. If you want sales or enquiries, a low CPM is only useful if the people seeing the advert go on to click and buy.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the total cost of the advert or campaign.
  2. Enter the number of impressions it received.
  3. Read off the cost per thousand impressions.

Working backwards from CPM

If you know the CPM, you can work out the other figures:

  • Cost = Impressions / 1,000 x CPM. A campaign of 200,000 impressions at a £4 CPM costs £800.
  • Impressions = Cost / CPM x 1,000. A budget of £600 at a £3 CPM buys 200,000 impressions.

For publishers, the same sum from the other side is called RPM: the revenue earned per thousand page views.

CPM and eCPM

Effective CPM, or eCPM, applies the same sum to advertising bought another way. If you paid per click and spent £200 for adverts that were shown 80,000 times, your eCPM is £2.50. It lets you compare campaigns bought on different pricing models.

Frequently asked questions

What is an impression?

One showing of an advert. The same person can account for several impressions.

Why do CPMs vary so much?

Price depends on the audience, the platform, the ad format and the time of year. Narrowly targeted audiences and busy periods such as the run-up to Christmas cost more.

What is CPC?

CPC, cost per click, is the average amount you pay each time someone clicks your advert. It is the basis of pay-per-click advertising on search engines, shopping ads and social media.

CPC formula

CPC = Ad spend / Number of clicks

Worked example

You spend £800 and receive 1,600 clicks. Your average CPC is £0.50.

How much can you afford to pay for a click?

Multiply the profit from a sale by your conversion rate. If a sale leaves £30 of profit and 2% of clicks become sales, a click is worth 60p to you. Paying more than that loses money on the first order.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter what you spent on the campaign, ad group or keyword.
  2. Enter the number of clicks it received.

CPC, CPM and CTR are linked

If you buy advertising by the thousand impressions, you can still work out an effective cost per click. Divide the CPM by 1,000 to get the cost of one impression, then divide by the click-through rate. A £5 CPM with a 1% CTR is an effective CPC of 50p.

Average CPC and maximum CPC

On auction platforms you set the most you are willing to pay for a click. You are usually charged less than that, because the price depends on the next highest bidder, so your average CPC sits below your maximum bid.

Is a low CPC always good?

No. Cheap clicks that never convert cost more in the end than expensive clicks that do.

What affects CPC?

  • Competition: more advertisers bidding on the same search pushes the price up.
  • Relevance: platforms charge less for adverts that people find useful and click on.
  • Targeting: location, device, time of day and audience all change the price.

What is click-through rate?

Click-through rate, or CTR, is the percentage of people who click something after seeing it. It applies to adverts, organic search results, email links and buttons on a web page.

CTR formula

CTR = Clicks / Impressions x 100

Worked example

An advert is shown 12,000 times and clicked 240 times. Its CTR is 2%.

Why CTR matters

A higher CTR means your message matches what the audience is looking for. On pay-per-click platforms it can also lower what you pay, because adverts that are clicked more often are treated as more relevant. In organic search, a better title and description can win more clicks from the same ranking.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the number of clicks.
  2. Enter the number of impressions, meaning how many times the advert, link or search result was shown.
  3. Read off the click-through rate.

Ways to improve CTR

  • Match the wording to the search. Use the words your audience uses.
  • Lead with a clear benefit and include a price or offer where you can.
  • Test one change at a time, so you know what made the difference.
  • Narrow the audience. Showing an advert to fewer, more relevant people usually raises CTR.

For email, the same sum is used with delivered emails in place of impressions. Some senders also quote clicks as a share of opens, called click-to-open rate.

Typical ranges

As a rough guide, search adverts often see click-through rates of a few per cent, display banners a fraction of one per cent, and marketing emails somewhere between the two. Position matters too: the first result on a search page attracts far more clicks than the fifth.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good CTR?

It depends on the channel. Search adverts usually get a much higher CTR than display banners, because people are already looking for something. Compare like with like.

Is a high CTR always good?

Not if the clicks don't convert. An advert that attracts the wrong visitors costs money without producing sales.

Conversion rate is the percentage of visitors who complete the action you want, such as placing an order, filling in a form or subscribing to a newsletter.

Your website has 8,000 visitors in a month and takes 200 orders. Your conversion rate is 2.5%.

Raising conversion rate increases sales without paying for more traffic. A shop converting 2.5% of 8,000 visitors takes 200 orders. At 3%, the same visitors give 240 orders: a fifth more sales from the same advertising spend.

Ways to improve conversion rate

  • Make pages load quickly, especially on mobile.

What is customer acquisition cost?

Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is the average amount you spend to win one new customer. It counts everything spent on bringing customers in, not only advertising.

CAC formula

CAC = (Marketing spend + Sales costs) / New customers

Use spending and new customers from the same period.

Worked example

In a quarter you spend £9,000 on marketing and £6,000 on sales staff and tools, £15,000 in all, and win 300 new customers. Your CAC is £50.

CAC and lifetime value

CAC only means something next to what a customer is worth. Many businesses aim for a customer lifetime value of around three times CAC. If the two figures are close, growth is costing nearly as much as it earns.

  2. Enter the sales costs for the same period, such as salaries and commission.

CAC payback period

The payback period is how long a customer takes to repay what it cost to win them. Divide CAC by the gross profit the customer brings in each month. With a CAC of £50 and £10 of monthly gross profit, payback takes 5 months. The shorter the payback, the less cash a business needs to fund its growth.

Should existing customers be counted?

No. CAC measures the cost of winning new customers. Spending on keeping existing ones is a retention cost.

Blended CAC divides all spending by all new customers, including those who arrived through word of mouth or search at no cost. Paid CAC counts only customers won through paid channels. Paid CAC is higher, and it is the better guide to what the next customer from advertising will cost.

CAC and CPA

CPA is usually measured for one campaign and can count any conversion, such as a lead. CAC covers all sales and marketing costs and counts only new paying customers, so it is normally higher.

Customer lifetime value, or CLV, is the total gross profit you can expect from an average customer for as long as they keep buying. It tells you how much you can afford to spend to win and keep a customer.

What is churn rate?

Churn rate is the percentage of customers who stop buying or cancel during a period. It matters most to subscription businesses, where income depends on customers staying.

Churn rate = Customers lost / Customers at start x 100

Retention rate = 100 - Churn rate

Customers who joined during the period are left out. Only count losses from the group you started with.

You begin the month with 1,200 subscribers and 60 cancel. Your monthly churn rate is 5% and your retention rate is 95%.

Monthly churn adds up

A monthly figure that looks small becomes large over a year. At 5% a month, only about 54% of customers are still with you after twelve months, because each month's loss is taken from a smaller group.

Customer churn and revenue churn

Customer churn counts people. Revenue churn counts the income they took with them. The two can differ sharply: losing one large customer may matter more than losing ten small ones. What is a good churn rate?

It depends on the market and the price. Low-cost consumer subscriptions lose customers far faster than contracts with large businesses. Your own trend over time is the most useful guide.

  • Ask leaving customers why, and look for the reasons that repeat.
  • Help new customers get value quickly in their first weeks.

What is ROI?

Return on investment, or ROI, is the profit from an investment shown as a percentage of what it cost. It lets you compare projects of different sizes on the same basis, whether that is new equipment, a marketing campaign or a stock purchase.

ROI formula

ROI = (Amount returned - Amount invested) / Amount invested x 100

Worked example

You spend £4,000 on a trade show and it brings in £5,200 of gross profit. The profit is £1,200, an ROI of 30%.

Getting a fair figure

  • Count all the costs, including staff time, fees and delivery.
  • Use profit, not sales, for the amount returned when you are measuring marketing. Revenue alone overstates the return.
  • Remember time. ROI takes no account of how long the return took. 30% in six months is better than 30% in three years.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the total amount invested, including every cost.
  2. Enter the total amount returned.
  3. Read off the profit or loss and the ROI as a percentage.

Annualised ROI

To compare investments held for different lengths of time, convert ROI to a yearly rate. Add 1 to the ROI as a decimal, raise the result to the power of 1 divided by the number of years, and subtract 1. An ROI of 30% over 2 years is 1.3 to the power of 0.5, less 1, which is about 14% a year.

ROI and ROAS

ROAS compares advertising revenue with advertising cost. ROI compares profit with all costs. A campaign with a ROAS of 4x can still have a negative ROI if the margin is thin.

Frequently asked questions

Can ROI be negative?

Yes. A negative ROI means you got back less than you put in.

What is a good ROI?

One that beats what the money could have earned elsewhere at similar risk.

SEO_Body:
What is revenue per employee?

Revenue per employee is a company's revenue divided by its headcount. It is a rough measure of productivity: how much income the business produces for each person it employs.

Revenue per employee formula

Revenue per employee = Annual revenue / Number of employees

Worked example

A business turns over £1,500,000 a year with 12 staff. Its revenue per employee is £125,000.

How to use the figure

The number varies widely between industries. Software and wholesale businesses can produce high revenue with few staff, while restaurants, care and retail need many more people for the same turnover. Compare yourself with similar businesses, and watch how your own figure changes from year to year.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the revenue for the last full year.
  2. Enter the average number of employees during that year, as full-time equivalents.
  3. Read off the revenue per employee.

What moves the figure

Revenue per employee rises when sales grow faster than headcount. That can come from better tools, automation, higher prices or outsourcing work that used to be done in-house. It falls when a business hires ahead of growth, which is normal for a company investing in new products or markets.

Outsourcing can flatter the figure: a firm that uses contractors and agencies will show higher revenue per employee than one doing the same work with its own staff. For a fairer comparison, look at profit per employee too.

Frequently asked question

Should contractors be included?

For a like-for-like view of productivity, yes, as full-time equivalents. Published company figures usually count employees only, so check what a benchmark includes before you compare.

Frequently asked questions

How should I count part-time staff?

Convert them to full-time equivalents. Two people each working half the week count as one.

Is higher always better?

Not on its own. A very high figure can mean the team is stretched. Look at profit per employee as well, because revenue says nothing about costs.
Short_Desc: Average revenue generated by each employee.

SEO_Body:
What is staff turnover?

Staff turnover, also called employee or labour turnover, is the percentage of your workforce that leaves in a given period, usually a year.

Staff turnover formula

Average employees = (Employees at start + Employees at end) / 2

Turnover rate = Leavers / Average employees x 100

Worked example

You start the year with 58 employees and end it with 62, an average of 60. During the year 9 people leave. Your staff turnover rate is 15%.

Why it matters

Replacing an employee costs money in recruitment, training and lost output while the role is empty or the new starter is learning. High turnover also puts pressure on the people who stay. Some sectors, such as hospitality and retail, normally see far higher turnover than others.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the number of employees who left during the period.
  2. Enter the headcount at the start and at the end of the period.
  3. Read off the average headcount and the turnover rate.

Going beyond one number

An overall rate is a starting point. It becomes useful when you break it down:

  • By team or manager, to find where people are leaving.
  • By length of service. Many leavers in the first year points to recruitment or induction problems.
  • By reason, gathered from exit interviews.

Some employers also measure a stability rate: the share of staff with more than a year's service who are still employed a year later.

Monthly and annual rates

If you measure turnover monthly, add the twelve monthly rates together for an annual figure. Do not multiply one month by twelve, because leavers are rarely spread evenly through the year.

Frequently asked questions

Who counts as a leaver?

Usually everyone who left, whatever the reason. Many employers also work out a separate figure for resignations only, as that is the part they can influence.

Is some turnover healthy?

Yes. New people bring new skills, and a rate of zero is neither likely nor necessarily desirable.
Short_Desc: Employee turnover rate from leavers and average headcount.

What is the Bradford Factor?

The Bradford Factor is a score some employers use to measure sickness absence. It gives extra weight to frequent short absences, on the view that these disrupt work more than one longer absence of the same total length.

Bradford Factor formula

Bradford Factor = S x S x D

S is the number of separate spells of absence and D is the total number of days absent, usually over a rolling 52 weeks.

Worked example

An employee is off on 4 separate occasions totalling 9 days. Their score is 144 points. One single absence of the same nine days would score 9, and nine separate days off would score 729.

Trigger points

Employers set their own thresholds, so there is no standard scale. A policy might call for an informal chat at one score and a formal review at a higher one. Check your own organisation's absence policy for the figures it uses.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the number of separate spells of absence in the last 52 weeks.
  2. Enter the total number of working days lost in those spells.
  3. Read off the score.

SEO_Body:
What is FTE?

FTE stands for full-time equivalent. It expresses a workforce of full-time and part-time people as the number of full-time staff who would work the same hours. One FTE is one person working full-time hours.

FTE formula

Part-time FTE = Total part-time hours per week / Full-time hours per week

Total FTE = Full-time employees + Part-time FTE

Worked example

You employ 14 full-time staff, and your full-time week is 37.5 hours. Your part-time staff work 180 hours a week between them, which is 4.80 FTE. Your total headcount is 18.80 FTE.

What FTE is used for

  • Budgeting and workforce planning, where hours matter more than the number of people.
  • Comparing teams or branches with different mixes of full-time and part-time staff.
  • Measures such as revenue per employee.
  • Grant applications and official returns that ask for FTE figures.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the number of full-time employees.
  2. Add up the weekly hours of all your part-time staff and enter the total.
  3. Enter the number of hours in your standard full-time week.

FTE for one person

To find one part-time employee's FTE, divide their weekly hours by the full-time week. Someone working 22.5 hours in an organisation with a 37.5 hour week is 0.6 FTE. The same fraction is used to work out pro rata pay and holiday: 0.6 FTE of a £30,000 salary is £18,000.

Frequently asked question

Is FTE the same as headcount?

No. Headcount is the number of people. Ten staff who each work half the week are a headcount of 10 and an FTE of 5. Budgets usually use FTE, while office space and equipment depend on headcount.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as full-time hours?

Whatever your organisation's standard full-time week is. In the UK that is commonly between 35 and 40 hours.

Can one person be more than 1 FTE?

Not normally. Overtime is usually left out, and each person counts as 1.0 at most.
Short_Desc: Headcount as full-time equivalents.

SEO_Body:
What is the payback period?

The payback period is the time it takes for the cash an investment brings in to equal what it cost. Businesses use it as a quick test of risk: the sooner the money is back, the less can go wrong in the meantime.

Payback period formula

Payback period = Initial investment / Net cash inflow per year

This assumes the same inflow every year.

Worked example

A new machine costs £24,000 and saves £7,500 a year. It pays for itself in 3.2 years, or 38.4 months.

Strengths and limits

  • Simple and quick. It needs only two figures.
  • Ignores what happens next. An investment that pays back in three years and then keeps earning for ten looks the same as one that stops after three.
  • Ignores the time value of money. Cash received later is worth less than cash today. Net present value takes that into account.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the upfront cost of the investment.
  2. Enter the net cash it brings in each year: extra income or savings, less running costs.
  3. Read off the payback period in years and months.

When cash flows are uneven

If the yearly inflow changes, add up the inflows year by year until the total reaches the cost. An investment of £24,000 that returns £5,000, £8,000 and £11,000 in its first three years has recovered exactly £24,000 at the end of year three.

Discounted payback

A stricter version reduces each year's inflow to its value today before adding them up. It always gives a longer payback than the simple method.

Payback and return on investment

The two measures answer different questions. Payback tells you how soon the money comes back. ROI tells you how much you gain in total. A project can pay back quickly and earn little afterwards, or pay back slowly and be very profitable over its life.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good payback period?

Shorter is safer. Many small businesses look for two to three years on equipment, but the right limit depends on how long the asset will last.
Short_Desc: How long an investment takes to pay for itself.

SEO_Body:
What is burn rate?

Burn rate is the amount of cash a business uses up each month. It matters most to start-ups and to any company spending more than it earns, because it shows how long the money will last.

Burn rate formula

Monthly burn rate = (Starting cash - Current cash) / Months

Cash runway = Current cash / Monthly burn rate

This is net burn: what you spend less what you take in.

Worked example

Your bank balance has fallen from £180,000 to £120,000 over 6 months. You are burning £10,000 a month, which leaves a runway of 12.0 months at the current rate.

Gross burn and net burn

Gross burn is everything you spend in a month. Net burn takes off the income you received. A business spending £40,000 a month and taking £30,000 in sales has a gross burn of £40,000 and a net burn of £10,000. Runway depends on net burn.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter your cash balance at the start of the period.
  2. Enter your cash balance now.
  3. Enter the number of months between the two.

Use bank balances, not profit figures. Burn rate is about cash.

How much runway is enough?

Investors and advisers often suggest keeping 12 to 18 months of runway, because raising money or reaching profitability usually takes longer than planned. Recalculate each month: burn tends to creep up as a business hires, and runway shortens faster than expected.

Default alive or default dead

A useful test for a young company is whether, at the current rate of growth and spending, it will reach profitability before the cash runs out. If revenue is rising faster than costs, burn falls each month and the runway is longer than the simple sum suggests.

Extending your runway

  • Cut or delay costs that do not bring in customers.
  • Collect payments sooner and agree longer terms with suppliers.
  • Raise prices or focus on the most profitable products.
  • Start fundraising well before the cash runs low, as it usually takes months.
Short_Desc: Monthly cash burn and how many months of cash remain.

What is torque?

Torque is a turning force. It is the force applied multiplied by its distance from the point of rotation, which is why a longer spanner makes a tight bolt easier to undo. A force of 10 newtons applied at the end of a 1 metre lever produces a torque of 10 newton metres.

Where torque figures are used

  • Tightening bolts. Wheel nuts, cylinder head bolts and bicycle components all have a specified torque. Too loose and they can work free, too tight and threads or parts can be damaged.
  • Engines and motors. Torque describes pulling power: how strongly an engine can turn the wheels at a given speed.
  • Power tools. Drill drivers and impact wrenches are rated by the torque they can deliver.

Worked example

A car handbook gives the wheel nut torque as 110 Nm, but your torque wrench is marked in pound-feet. Divide 110 by 1.3558 to get 81.1 lb-ft, and set the wrench to 81.

Is lb-ft the same as ft-lb?

For torque, yes. Both mean pounds of force multiplied by feet of distance. Strictly, foot-pound is also a unit of energy, which is why engineers prefer pound-foot for torque.

Should I always use a torque wrench?

For anything safety related, such as wheels, brakes and suspension, yes. Always use the figure in the manufacturer's manual.

What is force?

A force is a push or a pull. It is what makes an object speed up, slow down or change direction. Newton's second law states that force equals mass multiplied by acceleration, so a newton is defined as the force that accelerates a one kilogram mass at one metre per second squared.

Force and weight

Weight is the force of gravity on an object. On Earth, a mass of 1 kg weighs about 9.81 newtons, which is one kilogram-force. That is why loads are sometimes loosely given in kilograms: a rope rated at 10 kN will hold a static load of roughly 1,020 kg.

Worked example

A climbing carabiner is marked 24 kN. In pounds-force that is 24 x 224.81, or about 5,395 lbf, and in kilograms-force it is about 2,447 kgf.

  • Pounds-force: The imperial unit, written lbf: the weight of one pound under standard gravity.

Is a pound a unit of force or mass?

Both names exist. The pound (lb) is a unit of mass and the pound-force (lbf) is the weight of that mass. In everyday use people say pounds for either.

Why do ratings use kilonewtons and not kilograms?

Because a moving or falling load exerts far more force than its weight. A rating in kN describes the force the equipment can withstand, however it is produced.

SEO_Body:
What is frequency?

Frequency is how often something repeats in a given time. It is measured in hertz, the number of complete cycles per second. Sound, radio waves, alternating current and the vibration of a guitar string are all described by their frequency.

Everyday frequencies

  • 50 Hz: mains electricity in the UK and Europe. North America uses 60 Hz.
  • 20 Hz to 20 kHz: the range of human hearing.
  • 440 Hz: the note A above middle C, used to tune instruments.
  • 88 to 108 MHz: FM radio.
  • 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz: the two main Wi-Fi bands.

Frequency and rpm

Rotational speed is a frequency too. Divide revolutions per minute by 60 to get hertz. An engine turning at 3,000 rpm completes 50 revolutions each second, which is 50 Hz.

About the units

  • Hertz: One cycle per second, written Hz. UK mains electricity alternates at 50 Hz.
  • Kilohertz: 1,000 Hz. Used for audio and for AM radio.
  • Megahertz: One million Hz. Used for FM radio and older computer processors.
  • Gigahertz: One thousand million Hz. Used for Wi-Fi, mobile networks and processor speeds.
  • Revolutions per minute: How many full turns something makes in a minute. 60 rpm is 1 Hz.

Period

The period is the time one cycle takes, and it is 1 divided by the frequency. A 50 Hz supply has a period of 0.02 seconds, or 20 milliseconds. A 1 kHz tone has a period of 1 millisecond.

Frequently asked questions

How is frequency related to wavelength?

They are inversely related. The higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength. For radio waves, wavelength in metres is roughly 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz.

Is a higher GHz processor always faster?

Not necessarily. Clock speed is one factor, alongside the number of cores and the design of the chip.

Megabits and megabytes are not the same

Broadband is sold in megabits per second (Mbps), but files are measured in megabytes (MB). There are 8 bits in a byte, so divide a speed in Mbps by 8 to see how many megabytes arrive each second. This is the reason a download on an 80 Mbps connection shows about 10 MB/s, not 80.

You have a 100 Mbps connection and want to download a 4 GB file. 100 Mbps is 12.5 MB/s. The file is 4,000 MB, so it takes 4,000 divided by 12.5, which is 320 seconds, or a little over 5 minutes at full speed.

What speed do you need?

  • Video calls and HD streaming: around 5 Mbps per stream.
  • 4K streaming: around 25 Mbps per stream.
  • A busy household: add up what is likely to be in use at once.

These are typical figures quoted by streaming services. Upload speed, which is often much lower than download, matters for video calls and backing up files.

Wi-Fi signal, the number of devices sharing the connection, the time of day and the speed of the server at the other end all reduce it.

Is Mb the same as MB?

No. A lower-case b means bits and a capital B means bytes.

What is illuminance?

Illuminance is the amount of light landing on a surface. It is different from the light a lamp gives out, which is measured in lumens. The same lamp produces a high illuminance on a desk just below it and a much lower one on the far wall, because the light spreads out as it travels.

Lux and foot-candles

Both units describe lumens per unit of area. Lux uses square metres and foot-candles use square feet. As a square metre is about 10.76 square feet, one foot-candle equals 10.76 lux. For a quick estimate, multiply foot-candles by 10.

  • Lux: The metric unit of illuminance: one lumen falling on one square metre. Used in the UK and Europe.
  • Foot-candles: One lumen falling on one square foot, written fc. Used in the United States.

Where the conversion comes up

Lighting standards and product data from the United States are usually written in foot-candles, while British and European guidance uses lux. Photographers, film crews, growers using horticultural lighting and anyone comparing an American lighting specification with a European one need to move between the two. Why does light fall off with distance?

Light spreads over a larger area as it travels. Doubling the distance from a small source spreads the same light over four times the area, so the illuminance drops to a quarter.

How do I measure lux?

With a light meter, also called a lux meter, placed on the surface you want to measure. Phone apps give a rough reading.

How do lumens relate to lux?

Divide the lumens reaching a surface by its area in square metres. 1,000 lumens spread evenly over 10 m² gives 100 lux.

SEO_Body:
What is flow rate?

Flow rate is the volume of liquid or gas passing a point in a given time. It tells you how quickly a tap fills a bath, how much water a pump can move or how fast a pond is circulated.

How to measure the flow from a tap

Hold a measuring jug or a bucket of known size under the tap, turn it on fully and time how long it takes to fill. Divide the volume in litres by the time in seconds and multiply by 60. A 10 litre bucket that fills in 40 seconds means a flow of 15 litres per minute.

Typical household flow rates

  • Kitchen or basin tap: 4 to 10 litres per minute.
  • Electric shower: 3 to 8 litres per minute, depending on its power and the season.
  • Mixer or power shower: 8 to 15 litres per minute or more.
  • Garden hose: around 15 litres per minute.

These are typical ranges and vary with water pressure.

About the units

  • Litres per minute: The usual unit for taps, showers and domestic pumps in the UK.
  • Litres per second: 60 litres per minute. Used for larger pumps and drainage.
  • Cubic metres per hour: 1,000 litres an hour. Used for pool pumps, ventilation and industrial plant.
  • UK gallons per minute: 4.546 litres per minute.
  • US gallons per minute: 3.785 litres per minute, written gpm on American products.

Frequently asked questions

Is flow rate the same as water pressure?

No. Pressure is the force pushing the water and flow rate is the amount that comes out. Good pressure through a narrow pipe can still give a poor flow.

Which gallon do American products use?

The US gallon. A shower head rated at 2.5 gpm in the United States delivers about 9.5 litres per minute.

SEO_Body:
How to work out how much paint you need

The amount of paint depends on three things: the area of the walls, the number of coats and how far a litre of the paint goes. Measure the width of each wall you are painting and add them together, then multiply by the height of the room. Take off the area of doors and windows, because you will not be painting those.

Paint formula

Area to paint = (Total wall length x Wall height) - Doors and windows

Litres needed = Area to paint x Number of coats / Coverage

Worked example

A room has 14 m of wall in total and the walls are 2.4 m high, which is 33.6 m². Taking off 3.5 m² for a door and a window leaves 30.1 m² to paint. With 2 coats of a paint that covers 12 m² per litre, you need 5.0 litres. That is a 5 litre tin with nothing to spare, so a small extra tin is sensible.

Typical sizes and coverage

  • A standard internal door is about 1.6 m² and an average window is about 1.5 to 2 m².
  • Most emulsions cover 10 to 13 m² per litre. The figure for your paint is printed on the tin.
  • Bare plaster, textured walls and strong colour changes all use more paint.

How many coats?

Two coats is normal for walls. New plaster needs a thinned mist coat first, which soaks in and seals the surface. Painting a pale colour over a dark one may take three coats, or a coat of primer and two of colour.

Frequently asked questions

Does this work for ceilings?

Yes. Enter the length of the ceiling as the wall length and its width as the height, and set doors and windows to 0.

How much extra should I buy?

About 10% more than the result covers spills, the paint left in the roller and tray, and touch-ups later. Keeping some from the same batch avoids slight colour differences.
Short_Desc: Litres of paint needed for your walls and number of coats.

SEO_Body:
How many rolls of wallpaper do I need?

A standard roll of wallpaper sold in the UK is 10.05 metres long and 0.53 metres wide, so it covers a little over 5 m². This calculator divides the area of your walls by the area of a roll and adds an allowance for trimming and for lining up the pattern.

How to use the calculator

  1. Measure the width of each wall you are papering and add them up.
  2. Measure the height from skirting board to ceiling.
  3. Check the roll size on the label and change it if it is not the standard size.

Wallpaper formula

Wall area = Distance around the room x Wall height

Rolls = Wall area x (1 + Allowance / 100) / (Roll length x Roll width), rounded up.

Worked example

The walls to be papered measure 14 m around and are 2.4 m high, an area of 33.6 m². One roll covers 5.33 m². Adding 15% for waste and pattern matching, you need 8 rolls.

Pattern repeat

A plain or random-match paper wastes very little, and 10% is usually enough. A paper with a large pattern has to be lined up from one strip to the next, so part of every strip is cut off and thrown away. The bigger the repeat printed on the label, the more you lose: allow 15% to 25%, or an extra roll for a repeat of more than 50 cm.

Tips before you buy

  • Buy all the rolls at once and check that the batch number on each label is the same. Colours vary between batches.
  • Measure the height at several points. Ceilings are rarely level.
  • For a feature wall, enter the width of that one wall as the distance around the room.
  • Many retailers will refund unopened rolls, so one spare is cheap insurance.

Frequently asked questions

Should I deduct doors and windows?

Usually not. The strips above a door and around a window still use most of a length, and the leftover gives you a margin for mistakes.
Short_Desc: Number of wallpaper rolls needed for a room.

SEO_Body:
How to calculate the number of tiles

Work out the area you are tiling in square metres, divide it by the area of one tile, and add a percentage for the tiles that will be cut at the edges or broken. This calculator does all three steps and rounds the answer up to a whole tile.

How to use the calculator

  1. Measure the length and width of the floor, or the width and height of the wall, in metres.
  2. Enter the size of one tile in centimetres.
  3. Choose an allowance for cuts and breakages.

Tile formula

Area = Length x Width

Tiles = Area / (Tile length x Tile width) x (1 + Allowance / 100)

Tile sizes are entered in centimetres and converted to metres for you.

Worked example

A bathroom floor measures 3.2 m by 2.5 m, an area of 8.00 m². Using tiles of 30 cm by 30 cm, there are 11.1 tiles to the square metre. With 10% added for cuts and breakages, you need 98 tiles.

How much extra to allow

  • 10% for a simple square or rectangular area laid in straight rows.
  • 15% for a diagonal or herringbone layout, a room with lots of corners, or large-format tiles.
  • Keep a few spare tiles after the job. A matching tile may be impossible to find later if one cracks.

Tiles sold by the box

Tiles are usually sold in boxes that cover a stated area. Divide the number of tiles you need by the number in a box and round up. Check that every box has the same batch and shade number.

Frequently asked questions

Should I allow for grout lines?

Grout joints of 2 to 3 mm make very little difference to the count, so the calculator ignores them. That adds a small safety margin.

What about an L-shaped room?

Split it into two rectangles, work out each one and add the results.
Short_Desc: Number of tiles needed for a floor or wall.

SEO_Body:
How to work out how much flooring you need

Laminate, engineered wood and click vinyl are sold in packs, and each pack states the area it covers. Measure the room at its longest and widest points, multiply the two to get the area, add an allowance for offcuts and divide by the coverage of a pack.

How to use the calculator

  1. Measure the room at its longest and widest points.
  2. Enter the coverage printed on the pack, in square metres.
  3. Set the allowance for waste and enter the price of a pack.

Flooring formula

Floor area = Room length x Room width

Packs = Floor area x (1 + Allowance / 100) / Coverage per pack, rounded up.

Worked example

A living room is 4.5 m long and 3.6 m wide, so the floor area is 16.20 m². Each pack covers 2.22 m². With 10% added for waste, you need 9 packs. At £32 a pack, the flooring costs £288.

How much waste to allow

  • 5% to 10% for boards laid straight in a simple rectangular room.
  • 10% to 15% for rooms with alcoves, chimney breasts or several doorways.
  • 15% or more for herringbone or diagonal patterns.

Other things to budget for

The boards are only part of the cost. You may also need underlay, a damp-proof membrane on a concrete floor, door bars for each doorway, and beading or new skirting boards to cover the expansion gap at the edges. Leave unopened packs in the room for at least 48 hours before fitting, so the boards adjust to the temperature and humidity.

Frequently asked questions

My room is not a rectangle. What do I do?

Divide it into rectangles, work out the area of each and add them up. Enter the total as the length, with a width of 1.

Does this work for carpet?

No. Carpet is sold off a roll of fixed width, usually 4 or 5 metres, so it is priced by the length cut.
Short_Desc: Packs of laminate, vinyl or wood flooring for a room.
