SEO_Body:
How to calculate concrete volume

Concrete is ordered by volume, in cubic metres. For a rectangular slab, multiply the length by the width by the depth, with all three in metres. Depth is normally measured in millimetres, so the calculator converts it for you.

How to use the calculator

  1. Measure the length and width of the slab in metres.
  2. Enter the depth of concrete in millimetres.
  3. Leave the allowance at 10% unless your supplier advises otherwise.

For a circular base, work out the area as 3.14 times the radius squared, enter that as the length and set the width to 1.

Concrete formula

Volume (m³) = Length (m) x Width (m) x Depth (mm) / 1,000

Concrete to order = Volume x (1 + Allowance / 100)

Worked example

A shed base is 4 m long, 3 m wide and 100 mm deep. The volume is 1.20 m³. Adding 10% for uneven ground and spillage, you should order 1.32 m³, which weighs about 3.17 tonnes.

Typical slab depths

  • 75 mm to 100 mm: paths, patios and bases for small sheds.
  • 100 mm: a base for a larger shed, summerhouse or greenhouse.
  • 100 mm to 150 mm: driveways and garage floors, often with steel mesh.

These are common guide figures. The right depth depends on the ground and the load, and structural work should follow an engineer's or building control's advice.

Ready-mix, mix on site or bags?

For anything over about one cubic metre, ready-mixed concrete delivered by lorry is usually easiest. Smaller jobs can be mixed on site from cement and ballast, or from pre-mixed bags for very small quantities such as fence posts. Remember the sub-base: a slab normally sits on a layer of compacted hardcore, which you need to order separately.

Frequently asked questions

Why add 10%?

The ground is never perfectly level, formwork bows slightly and some concrete is always lost. Running short part-way through a pour is far more costly than having a little left over.
Short_Desc: Cubic metres of concrete for a slab, base or path.

How to work out how much gravel you need

Gravel is sold by weight, but the amount you need depends on volume. Multiply the length of the area by its width and by the depth of gravel to get cubic metres, then multiply by the weight of a cubic metre of the gravel you are buying.

Gravel formula

Volume (m³) = Length (m) x Width (m) x Depth (mm) / 1,000

Tonnes = Volume x Weight per cubic metre

Worked example

A drive is 6 m long and 3 m wide, and you want gravel 50 mm deep. The volume is 0.90 m³. At 1.6 tonnes per m³, that is 1.44 tonnes of gravel, or 2 bags of 850 kg each.

How deep should gravel be?

  • Paths and borders: 30 mm to 40 mm is enough for foot traffic.
  • Driveways: around 50 mm, on a firm compacted sub-base.
  • The depth should be at least twice the size of the stones. A 20 mm gravel needs 40 mm or more to cover properly.

Too deep is as much a problem as too shallow: feet and tyres sink in.

Bulk bags and loose loads

A bulk bag, sometimes called a tonne bag or dumpy bag, usually holds between 800 kg and 900 kg. Check the weight with your supplier and change the figure above if it differs. For larger jobs, a loose tipped load is often cheaper per tonne, provided a lorry can reach the site.

Frequently asked questions

Does the type of stone matter?

Yes. Dense stone such as granite weighs more per cubic metre than slate chippings or lightweight aggregates. Wet gravel also weighs more than dry.

Do I need a membrane?

A weed-control membrane under the gravel is usual. It stops weeds and keeps the stone from mixing with the soil.
Short_Desc: Tonnes and bulk bags of gravel for a drive or path.

SEO_Body:
How to calculate the area of a room

For a rectangular room, measure the length and the width in metres and multiply them together. The answer is the floor area in square metres. Measure wall to wall at floor level, and ignore skirting boards.

How to use the calculator

  1. Measure the longest wall and enter it as the length.
  2. Measure the wall at right angles to it and enter that as the width.
  3. Read off the area in square metres and square feet.

A laser measure is quicker and more accurate than a tape in a furnished room.

Area formula

Area (m²) = Length (m) x Width (m)

Area (sq ft) = Area (m²) x 10.7639

Distance around the room = 2 x (Length + Width)

Worked example

A bedroom is 4.2 m long and 3.5 m wide. Its floor area is 14.70 m², which is 158.2 sq ft. The distance around the walls is 15.40 m.

Rooms that are not rectangles

  • L-shaped rooms: split the floor into two rectangles, work out each area and add them together.
  • Alcoves and bay windows: measure them as separate rectangles and add them on.
  • Chimney breasts: measure the area they take up and subtract it.

What the figures are used for

Floor area tells you how much flooring, underlay or underfloor heating to buy, and estate agents quote it when describing a property. The distance around the room is what you need for skirting board, coving and wallpaper. For paint, multiply the distance around the room by the ceiling height to get the wall area.

Frequently asked questions

I measured in feet. Can I still use this?

Convert each measurement to metres first by multiplying feet by 0.3048. A room of 14 feet by 12 feet is 4.27 m by 3.66 m.

How accurate do I need to be?

Measure to the nearest centimetre. A small error on each side becomes a larger error once the two are multiplied.
Short_Desc: Floor area in square metres and square feet.

SEO_Body:
How to convert amps to watts

Power in watts is the current in amps multiplied by the voltage. Amps measure how much electricity is flowing, volts measure the pressure pushing it, and watts measure the rate at which energy is used.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the current in amps, from the rating plate, a fuse or a clamp meter reading.
  2. Check the voltage. Leave it at 230 for UK mains, or enter 12 for a car or caravan system.
  3. Read off the power in watts and kilowatts.

How many watts can a 13 amp socket supply?

About 3,000 watts. A double socket is rated for 13 amps across both outlets on most designs, not 26.

Amps to watts formula

Watts = Amps x Volts

This applies to direct current and to simple resistive loads on mains electricity, such as heaters, kettles and filament lamps.

Worked example

A standard UK plug is fused at up to 13 A. At a mains voltage of 230 V, the most a single socket can supply is 2,990 W, or 2.99 kW. That is why a 3 kW kettle or fan heater is the largest appliance you will find on a 13 amp plug.

Common currents at 230 volts

CurrentPowerTypical use
3 A690 WFuse for lamps and small appliances
6 A1,380 WLighting circuit
13 A2,990 WMaximum for a UK plug
16 A3,680 WImmersion heater circuit
32 A7,360 WRing main or cooker circuit

Motors and other appliances

Appliances with motors or electronic power supplies draw slightly more current than this sum suggests, because of an effect called power factor. For those, real power is amps times volts times the power factor, a number between 0 and 1. The rating plate on the appliance gives the true figure.

Frequently asked questions

Is UK mains 230 V or 240 V?

The official figure is 230 volts, within an allowed range. In practice many UK homes measure closer to 240 volts.
Short_Desc: Power in watts from current in amps and voltage.

What is Ohm's law?

Ohm's law describes how voltage, current and resistance are related in an electrical circuit. The current through a conductor is the voltage across it divided by its resistance. It is named after the German physicist Georg Ohm, who published it in 1827.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the voltage across the component or circuit.
  2. Enter its resistance in ohms.
  3. Read off the current and the power it will dissipate.

For a resistor, check that the power is within its rating. A common small resistor is rated at a quarter of a watt.

Ohm's law formulas

Current (A) = Voltage (V) / Resistance (Ω)

The same relationship can be rearranged to find either of the other values:

Voltage = Current x Resistance

Resistance = Voltage / Current

Power follows from it: Power (W) = Voltage x Current.

Worked example

A 12 V supply is connected across a resistance of 6 Ω. The current is 2 A, and the power used is 24.00 W.

An everyday way to picture it

Think of water in a pipe. Voltage is the pressure pushing the water, current is how much water flows, and resistance is how narrow the pipe is. More pressure pushes more water through. A narrower pipe lets less through at the same pressure.

Where Ohm's law is used

  • Choosing a resistor to limit the current through an LED.
  • Working out how much current a heating element will draw.
  • Finding the voltage lost along a length of cable.
  • Checking that a component will not be overloaded.

Frequently asked questions

Does Ohm's law work for everything?

No. It holds for resistors and most metal conductors at a steady temperature. Components such as LEDs, diodes and filament lamps do not have a fixed resistance, so the simple formula only gives an approximation.

What is an ohm?

The unit of resistance. One ohm lets one amp flow when one volt is applied.
Short_Desc: Current and power from voltage and resistance.

Lumens and watts measure different things

Lumens measure how much light a bulb gives out. Watts measure how much electricity it uses. With old filament bulbs the two went hand in hand, so people learned to judge brightness by wattage. Modern LED bulbs give the same light for a fraction of the power, so lumens are now the figure to shop by.

  2. Choose the type of bulb.

Lumens to watts formula

Watts = Lumens / Lumens per watt

Lumens per watt is the efficiency of the bulb, called luminous efficacy. It varies by technology and from one product to another.

Worked example

You want a bulb as bright as an old 60 watt filament bulb, which gives about 806 lm. An LED producing 100 lumens per watt needs only 8.1 W to give the same light.

  • Check the cap type and whether the bulb is dimmable.

Frequently asked questions

Why do two LED bulbs with the same lumens use different watts?

Efficiency differs between products. Newer and better-quality LEDs produce more light per watt.

SEO_Body:
How much light does a room need?

The amount of light falling on a surface is measured in lux. One lux is one lumen spread over one square metre. To find the total light a room needs, multiply its floor area by the lux level suited to what the room is used for.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the length and width of the room in metres.
  2. Choose the type of room.
  3. Enter the lumens of the bulbs you plan to use, from the packaging.

Room lighting formula

Lumens needed = Floor area (m²) x Lux level

Number of bulbs = Lumens needed / Lumens per bulb, rounded up.

Worked example

A living room measures 4.5 m by 3.6 m, a floor area of 16.20 m². At 150 lux it needs 2,430 lm of light. Using bulbs of 806 lm each, that is 4 bulbs.

Typical light levels for a home

  • 100 lux: hallways, landings and stairs.
  • 150 lux: living rooms and bedrooms, for relaxed general lighting.
  • 200 lux: bathrooms.
  • 300 lux: kitchens and utility rooms.
  • 500 lux: desks, workshops and anywhere detailed work is done.

Getting the lighting right

The total is a starting point. Dark walls and floors absorb light, so a room decorated in deep colours needs more. High ceilings also need more, because the light has further to travel. Several lower-powered lights spread around a room give a more even result than one bright fitting in the middle, and a dimmer lets you turn a bright room down in the evening.

Frequently asked questions

Do lamps and spotlights count?

Yes. Add up the lumens of every light source in the room.

What about task lighting?

Worktops, desks and mirrors benefit from their own light, such as under-cabinet strips or a desk lamp, on top of the general lighting.
Short_Desc: Lumens and number of bulbs needed to light a room.

How to work out the cost of running an appliance

Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour (kWh), often called a unit. One kWh is the energy used by a 1,000 watt appliance running for one hour. To find the cost, turn the appliance's watts into kilowatts, multiply by the hours it runs, and multiply by the price of a unit.

How to use the calculator

  1. Find the appliance's power in watts on its rating plate.
  2. Estimate how many hours a day it is actually running.
  3. Enter your unit rate in pence per kWh from your bill.

Electricity cost formula

kWh used = Watts / 1,000 x Hours

Cost = kWh used x Price per kWh

Worked example

A 2,000 W fan heater is used for 1.5 hours a day. It uses 3.00 kWh a day. At 28 p per kWh, that costs £0.84 a day, £25.55 a month or £306.60 over a full year of daily use.

Typical power of household appliances

ApplianceTypical power

Television50 to 150 W
Microwave oven700 to 1,200 W
Vacuum cleaner600 to 900 W
Fan heater2,000 W
Kettle2,200 to 3,000 W
Electric shower7,500 to 10,500 W

These are typical ranges. The rating plate on your own appliance gives its actual figure.

Why real costs can be lower

The wattage on the plate is the most an appliance draws. Fridges, ovens, irons and heaters with thermostats switch on and off to hold a temperature, and washing machines only heat for part of the cycle. For these, the energy label or a plug-in energy monitor gives a truer picture.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I find my electricity price?

Your unit rate, in pence per kWh, is on your bill and in your supplier's app. The daily standing charge is separate and is not affected by how much you use.

SEO_Body:
How much do LED bulbs save?

An LED bulb gives the same light as a halogen or filament bulb for a small fraction of the electricity. The saving depends on the difference in wattage, how many bulbs you change and how long they are on each day.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the wattage of the bulbs you have now and of the LEDs that will replace them.
  2. Enter how many bulbs you are changing and how long they are on each day.
  3. Enter your electricity price and the cost of one LED bulb.

LED savings formula

kWh saved per year = (Old watts - LED watts) x Number of bulbs x Hours per day x 365 / 1,000

Saving per year = kWh saved x Price per kWh

Worked example

A kitchen has 10 halogen spotlights of 50 W each, on for 4 hours a day. Replacing them with 5 W LEDs saves 657 kWh a year. At 28 p per kWh, that is £183.96 a year. If each LED costs £3, the new bulbs pay for themselves in 2.0 months.

Other benefits of LEDs

  • Longer life. A good LED is rated for 15,000 hours or more, compared with around 2,000 hours for a halogen, so you replace bulbs far less often.
  • Less heat. Halogen bulbs turn most of their energy into heat. LEDs run much cooler.
  • Choice of light colour, from warm white to daylight.

Things to check before you switch

Match the cap type (such as GU10, B22 or E27) and compare lumens to get the same brightness. If the lights are on a dimmer, buy dimmable LEDs and check that the dimmer is suitable for LED loads, as older dimmers can cause flicker. Low-voltage MR16 spotlights may also need a compatible transformer.

Frequently asked questions

Are halogen bulbs still sold?

Most mains-voltage halogen bulbs have been phased out of sale in the UK, so LED is now the usual replacement.
Short_Desc: Yearly saving from replacing old bulbs with LEDs.

SEO_Body:
What is a kilowatt-hour?

A kilowatt-hour, written kWh, is a unit of energy. It is the amount used by something with a power of one kilowatt (1,000 watts) running for one hour. Electricity and gas bills are charged per kWh, which is why suppliers also call it a unit.

How to use the calculator

  1. Enter the power of the appliance in watts.
  2. Enter how many hours it runs in a day.
  3. Read off the energy used per day, per month and per year.

If the power is given in kilowatts, multiply by 1,000 first: 2.2 kW is 2,200 watts.

kWh formula

kWh = Watts x Hours / 1,000

Dividing by 1,000 converts watts into kilowatts.

Worked example

A television with a power of 150 W is on for 5 hours a day. It uses 0.75 kWh a day, which is 22.8 kWh a month and 274 kWh a year.

Watts and kilowatt-hours are different things

Watts measure power: how fast energy is being used at any moment. Kilowatt-hours measure energy: the total used over a period. A 3,000 watt kettle has high power but runs for only a few minutes, so it uses little energy each time. A 100 watt appliance left on all day uses far more.

One kWh in everyday terms

One kilowatt-hour is roughly enough to:

  • run a 10 watt LED bulb for 100 hours;
  • run a 2,000 watt fan heater for 30 minutes;
  • boil a full 3,000 watt kettle about eight times, at two and a half minutes each;
  • run a 100 watt television for 10 hours.

Frequently asked questions

How do I turn kWh into cost?

Multiply by your unit price. At 28p per kWh, 10 kWh costs £2.80. Our Electricity Cost Calculator does this for you.

What is the difference between kW and kWh?

kW is power and kWh is energy. Power multiplied by time gives energy.

What is standby power?

Many devices keep drawing a little electricity when they are switched off at the remote but still plugged in. This is standby power, sometimes called vampire or phantom power. It runs things like remote control receivers, clocks, network connections and instant-on features.

How to use the calculator

  1. Add up the standby power of the devices you leave plugged in.
  2. Enter how many hours a day they sit on standby.
  3. Enter your electricity price in pence per kWh.

Standby cost formula

kWh per year = Standby watts x Hours per day x 365 / 1,000

Cost per year = kWh per year x Price per kWh

Worked example

A television, set-top box and games console together draw 8 W on standby and are left that way for 20 hours a day. Over a year that is 58.4 kWh, which costs £16.35 at 28 p per kWh.

Which devices use the most?

  • Low: modern televisions and phone chargers with nothing attached usually draw well under 1 watt.
  • Medium: smart speakers, printers, microwaves with clocks and older audio equipment draw a few watts.
  • Higher: set-top boxes, games consoles with instant-on enabled and older appliances can draw 10 watts or more.

Products sold in the UK and EU in recent years have to meet limits on standby power, so newer equipment is generally much better than old.

How to cut standby use

Switch devices off at the wall, or use an extension lead with individual switches so one press cuts power to several. Smart plugs can do it on a timer. Check the power settings on consoles and set-top boxes for an energy-saving standby mode. Leave on anything that needs to stay connected, such as a router or a recorder set to record.

Frequently asked questions

How do I measure standby power?

A plug-in energy monitor, which sits between the plug and the socket, shows the watts a device is drawing.
